questions.stem: What is JSON / XML Schema Modelling?
options: The practice of defining structured schemas for semi-structured formats such as JSON and XML
The practice of normalising documents into relational tables
The practice of storing behaviour with data in objects
The practice of partitioning documents by key
The practice of replaying document changes as events
questions.explanation: JSON / XML Schema Modelling defines the allowed structure, elements, datatypes and constraints of documents to ensure consistency, validation and interoperability.

questions.stem: What is the primary goal of JSON / XML Schema Modelling?
options: Optimising database storage
Providing a clear and enforceable contract for APIs, integration workflows and document-based systems
Supporting complex analytical joins
Eliminating redundancy through normal forms
Enabling relationship traversal
questions.explanation: Rather than focusing on database storage, the technique focuses on structured data exchange, giving systems an enforceable contract for the data they share.

questions.stem: Which rule might a Loan schema define for the Status field?
options: It must be a numeric value greater than zero
It must be a required string identifier
It must be one of a predefined set of values
It must be a nested object
It must be unique across all loans
questions.explanation: The example Loan schema defines LoanID as a required string, LoanAmount as a numeric field greater than zero and Status as one of a predefined set of values.

questions.stem: In the loan approval example, why might a bank use both JSON and XML?
options: Because JSON is required by regulators and XML by mobile apps
Because XML is faster to parse than JSON
Because JSON cannot represent nested objects
Because JSON serves mobile applications and partner integrations while a regulatory authority requires XML submissions
Because XML is needed for caching
questions.explanation: JSON provides agility for modern applications and partner APIs, while XML supports compliance, standards-based exchange and legacy integration required by regulators.

questions.stem: In the JSON loan representation, which fields are nested objects?
options: LoanID and Status
LoanAmount and InterestRate
Repayments and Branch
LoanID and LoanAmount
Customer and Officer
questions.explanation: The JSON loan has a nested Customer object with CustomerID and Name, a nested Officer object with OfficerID and Name, and LoanAmount and Status at the top level.

questions.stem: How does the XML representation of the loan relate to the JSON representation?
options: It preserves the same logical structure using nested tags under a root Loan element
It flattens all fields into attributes of a single tag
It stores the loan as a comma-separated string
It omits the Customer and Officer information
It uses a different set of field names
questions.explanation: The equivalent XML structures the same information using nested tags under a root Loan element, preserving the logical structure in XML syntax.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT listed as a strength of JSON and XML schemas?
options: Human readability and wide platform support
Optimisation for complex joins and analytical workloads
Self-describing documents and structured validation
Effectiveness for integration between distributed systems
Consistent interpretation of data by all participants
questions.explanation: Neither JSON nor XML is optimised for complex joins or analytical workloads; their purpose is structured data exchange rather than relational querying.

questions.stem: What limitation does JSON have on its own regarding data types?
options: It cannot store numbers
It cannot represent arrays
It lacks strict typing unless paired with a formal JSON Schema
It requires a root element for every document
It cannot be read by humans
questions.explanation: JSON by itself lacks strict typing; a formal JSON Schema is needed to enforce types and constraints.

questions.stem: What trade-off is associated with XML?
options: It cannot express nesting
It is not supported by regulators
It lacks any validation mechanism
It can be verbose and computationally heavier to process
It cannot be used for legacy integration
questions.explanation: XML is powerful and expressive but can be verbose and computationally heavier to process than JSON.

questions.stem: Why do normalisation forms not apply to JSON / XML Schema Modelling?
options: Because these formats have no data types
Because these formats are always stored in key–value databases
Because these formats cannot contain redundancy
Because these formats are governed by 6NF instead
Because these formats are hierarchical and document-centric rather than relational
questions.explanation: Designers may structure documents cleanly and avoid redundancy, but that is not governed by formal normal forms because the formats are hierarchical and document-centric.
